body.statement: Under \(d^\star\), let \(b_{n,\varepsilon}=\mathbb P_{d^\star}(G_n(\varepsilon)^c)\). On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)=\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\), and \[\frac{\sigma^2}{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}\preceq\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_{\varepsilon}\mid F)\preceq\frac{\sigma^2}{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma_k(d^\star)^{-1}.\] Unconditionally, \[R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)=\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\left[\mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}\operatorname{tr}((F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1})\right]+\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.\] Furthermore, \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le\min\{1,\delta_{n,\varepsilon}\}\), where \(\delta_{n,\varepsilon}=2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}\), and \[\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}\frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}\le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)\le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}+B^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.\] The upper bound also implies \[R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)\le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}(1+2\varepsilon)+2B^2q\exp\{-n\varepsilon^2/(3\mu^\star)\}.\]
body.proof_tex:
Write \(\Sigma=\Sigma_k(d^\star)\) and \(w_a=\Sigma^{-1/2}x_a\). The trace lemma makes \(\Sigma\) positive definite. Product randomization across units and the definition of \(\Sigma\) imply that the \(w_a\) are independent and
\[
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}]=I_q.
\]
The causal coefficient vector remains distinct from its observed-law identifying functional. In fact, linear response and conditional centering give
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]
 &=\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_ax_a^{\mathsf T}]\beta
   +\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_a\epsilon_a]\\
 &=\Sigma\beta+
   \mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[x_a\mathbb E(\epsilon_a\mid F)\right]
 =\Sigma\beta.
\end{aligned}
\]
Division by the invertible \(\Sigma\) therefore proves, rather than defines, \(\beta=\Sigma^{-1}\mathbb E_{d^\star}[x_aY_a]\).
Moreover, the exact-leverage proposition and the finiteness of the Boolean support imply
\[
 \lambda_{\max}(w_aw_a^{\mathsf T})=\|w_a\|_2^2
 =x_a^{\mathsf T}\Sigma^{-1}x_a\le\mu^\star
 \quad\text{almost surely}. \tag{4}
\]
Apply the cited matrix Chernoff result with \(K_a=w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}\), \(R=\mu^\star\), and
\[
 \mu_{\min}=\mu_{\max}
 =\lambda_{\min}(nI_q)=\lambda_{\max}(nI_q)=n.
\]
Put
\[
 h_+(t)=(1+t)\log(1+t)-t,
 \qquad
 h_-(t)=t+(1-t)\log(1-t).
\]
Both functions and their first derivatives vanish at zero, while, on \(0\le t\le1/2\),
\[
 h_+''(t)=\frac1{1+t}\ge\frac23,
 \qquad
 h_-''(t)=\frac1{1-t}\ge1.
\]
Twice integrating these inequalities gives \(h_+(t)\ge t^2/3\) and \(h_-(t)\ge t^2/2\ge t^2/3\). Since
\[
 \frac1n\sum_{a=1}^n w_aw_a^{\mathsf T}
 =\Sigma^{-1/2}(F^{\mathsf T}F/n)\Sigma^{-1/2},
\]
the union of the cited weak upper- and lower-tail events contains \(G_n(\varepsilon)^c\). Thus
\[
 b_{n,\varepsilon}
 \le2q\exp\!\left\{-\frac{n\varepsilon^2}{3\mu^\star}\right\}
 =\delta_{n,\varepsilon},
\]
and of course \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\le1\), proving the stated minimum bound.

On \(G_n(\varepsilon)\), the definition of that event gives
\[
 (1-\varepsilon)\Sigma\preceq F^{\mathsf T}F/n
 \preceq(1+\varepsilon)\Sigma. \tag{5}
\]
Because \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), both bounds are positive definite, so \(F^{\mathsf T}F\) is invertible there. Inverting (5), with reversal of Loewner order, yields
\[
 \frac1{n(1+\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}
 \preceq(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}
 \preceq\frac1{n(1-\varepsilon)}\Sigma^{-1}. \tag{6}
\]
On this event, the linear-response assumption gives
\[
 \widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta
 =(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}F^{\mathsf T}\epsilon.
\]
Conditional centering and conditional homoskedasticity consequently imply
\[
 \mathbb E[\widehat\beta_\varepsilon-\beta\mid F]=0,
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(\widehat\beta_\varepsilon\mid F)
 =\sigma^2(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}.
\]
Multiplying (6) by \(\sigma^2>0\) proves the asserted conditional covariance sandwich.

The event \(G_n(\varepsilon)\) is measurable with respect to \(F\). On it, conditional mean zero makes the conditional squared-error risk the trace of the displayed covariance. On its complement the estimator is identically zero, so its squared error is exactly \(\|\beta\|_2^2\). The two disjoint cases therefore give the exact unconditional decomposition
\[
 R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 =\sigma^2\mathbb E_{d^\star}\!\left[
 \mathbf 1_{G_n(\varepsilon)}
 \operatorname{tr}\{(F^{\mathsf T}F)^{-1}\}\right]
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}. \tag{7}
\]
Taking traces in (6), using \(\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma^{-1})=\Phi^\star\), multiplying by the indicator, and averaging gives
\[
 \frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n}
 \frac{1-b_{n,\varepsilon}}{1+\varepsilon}
 \le R_n(\beta,\sigma,\varepsilon)
 \le\frac{\sigma^2\Phi^\star}{n(1-\varepsilon)}
 +\|\beta\|_2^2b_{n,\varepsilon}.
\]
The coefficient-ball assumption replaces the final norm by \(B^2\). Finally, for \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\),
\[
 \frac1{1-\varepsilon}\le1+2\varepsilon,
\]
and substituting the Chernoff envelope for \(b_{n,\varepsilon}\) proves the last advertised upper bound. No distributional property of the noise beyond the two stated conditional moments has been used.
body.justification: The theorem verifies the exact Chernoff constant and keeps the fallback bias in the unconditional risk.
body.gap: Tropp2012 supplies the tail tool and HsuKakadeZhang2014 supplies general decompositions, but neither gives this product-Fourier leverage calibration or fallback branch.
body.consumer: The bound converts the exact population design into an auditable finite-sample precision guarantee.
